title: US-Canada Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse, Washington and Ankara Friction Grows Over Israeli Strikes in Syria
subhead: Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods after negotiations collapsed, deepening a rupture in the Western alliance. Separately, a US envoy says Israel struck Syria without notice and may have been baiting Turkey, exposing strain inside the anti-Iran coalition.

sections.heading: US-Canada Trade War Deepens After Talks Collapse
sections.body:
The United States and Canada fell deeper into a trade war on Saturday, with Washington imposing 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods after negotiations broke down in Washington late Friday, according to AP. President Donald Trump's import taxes hit roughly 5 percent of annual Canadian shipments to the US, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariffs protecting exposed industries, including steel, dairy, appliances and pulp and paper, and set September 8 as the start of retaliation.

Carney accused Washington of using economic integration as a weapon, saying its signature was written in pencil, and described the country as having been attacked. You are at war when you get attacked, he said. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer countered that Washington was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its longtime partner, saying the interest is in protecting American workers and supply chains. No further talks were planned, and AP reports a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties.
sections.whyItMatters: This is not a minor tariff dispute but a widening rupture between the two closest allies in the Western alliance, one that hits a shared border economy, raises prices on both sides, and signals that economic coercion is now being applied within the US alliance network itself.

sections.heading: Iran Threatens Gulf Oil Routes as US Tightens Economic War
sections.body:
Iran's newly installed head of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened Tehran's neighbors against joining new US efforts to squeeze the economy, saying Iran would retaliate in a seismic manner and target oil-shipping routes that serve as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz if neighbors join the economic war, AP reports. Rezaei, named this month in appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran's stance, called those neighbors enemies whose interests would be targeted.

On the US side, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled a new phase of secondary sanctions against nations and companies that do business with Iran, after President Trump promised an unprecedented level of economic warfare. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the pressure on social media, saying Iran has seen this movie before. AP also reports Egypt is attempting to revive US-Iran negotiations, and that France and Saudi Arabia are expected to discuss plans to bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely, even as Iraq and Iran say Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil transit the strait.
sections.whyItMatters: Tehran's explicit threat to hit alternative oil routes widens the conflict beyond the Strait of Hormuz, and the move toward secondary sanctions threatens to drag major Iran oil buyers, including China and India, into a direct confrontation over the terms of the war.

sections.heading: Israel-Turkey Tension in Syria Strains the US-Led Coalition
sections.body:
US ambassador to Turkiye and special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack accused Israel of carrying out military strikes in Syria this week without adequate warning, calling the attacks an unnecessary escalation and suggesting they may have been aimed at baiting the Turks, Al Jazeera reports. The strikes hit the Abu Duhur military base in northern Syria. Israeli officials insisted they shared intelligence with the US beforehand, and Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel had provided information to authorized parties prior to the strike on Tuesday.

Katz dismissed Barrack's comments as full of inaccuracies and contrary to the stance of President Trump, and Israel has stepped up threats against Turkiye in recent months, portraying it as a potential regional rival. Turkiye, which blasted the Israeli strikes as reckless, holds substantial influence in northern Syria. The episode exposes friction between Washington, its strongest regional ally in Israel, and Ankara, which the US has courted for years, even as both are nominally part of the broader US effort against Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: A public rift between Washington's envoy and Israel over a strike aimed, in the envoy's telling, at provoking Turkey shows the US-led coalition is not monolithic; Israel's own campaign in Syria now risks colliding with Turkish interests and with Washington's attempt to hold the anti-Iran coalition together.

sections.heading: Russia Strikes Kyiv and Kryvyi Rih as Ukraine Hits Krasnodar
sections.body:
Russian aerial strikes killed at least seven people in Ukraine on Saturday, a day after a Russian drone attack on a shopping centre in President Zelenskyy's hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed at least 16 and wounded about 130, Al Jazeera reports. In the capital, Kyiv, one person was killed and another wounded when ballistic missiles hit railway infrastructure overnight, with two more killed in a strike on the surrounding region. Ukraine's authorities reported further deaths in Zaporizhzhia, where one person was killed overnight and three in a daytime attack.

On the other side, a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's southern Krasnodar region killed three people, including two children. Ukrainian officials described the Kryvyi Rih assault as a double-tap strike, in which a second wave of jet-powered Shahed drones hit roughly 30 minutes after the first, apparently targeting emergency crews responding to the crowded mall. Zelenskyy accused Russia of a cowardly and deliberate attack on the shopping complex.
sections.whyItMatters: The Kryvyi Rih attack, aimed at rescue workers in a second wave, marks a grim escalation in Russia's campaign against civilian infrastructure, while Ukraine's reach into Krasnodar shows the two-way nature of the strike war as the battlefield remains frozen along much of the front.

sections.heading: Wildfires Detonate Unexploded World War Ordnance Across Europe
sections.body:
Wildfires sweeping parts of Europe are exposing and detonating buried bombs and mines left from both World War I and World War II, AP reports, as heat and drought spread across the continent. The blazes have burned through former battlefields and old munitions sites, triggering explosions that endanger both firefighters and residents and complicate containment efforts.

The phenomenon links the region's climate-driven wildfire season with the physical residue of its 20th-century wars, forcing European governments to account for unexploded ordnance as a recurring hazard rather than a settled legacy. The story underlines how Europe's chronic wildfire problem is now intersecting with a fresh security concern, in the same season in which the continent has dealt with record-low rivers and severe drought.
sections.whyItMatters: As climate-driven fires grow more frequent, the live munitions buried across Europe's former battlefields add a dangerous, long-ignored layer to disaster response, turning routine fire seasons into hazardous clearance operations and stretching already-strained emergency services.

bottomLine: The defining development of the day is the collapse of US-Canada talks into a 50 percent tariff war, marking the clearest economic rupture yet inside the Western alliance, while the US-led camp against Iran shows internal strain as Washington's envoy accuses Israel of provoking Turkey with strikes in Syria. Iran is widening its own threat to alternative oil routes in response to fresh US pressure, and the Russia-Ukraine drone war continues to escalate on both sides of the border. The broadest picture is one of simultaneous fragmentation, as economic, military and climate pressures erode alliances and supply chains once taken for granted.
